en: Oṃ.
The mind is said to be of two kinds: pure and indeed impure.
The impure is characterized by desire and volition; the pure is devoid of desire. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1)
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings;
it is held that when attached to sense objects it leads to bondage, and when free from sense objects it leads to liberation.
Since liberation is desired for this mind when it is without an object, therefore the seeker of liberation must constantly make the mind free from objects. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3)

When the mind, with its attachment to sense objects cast off and completely restrained within the heart, attains the state beyond the mind (unmanībhāva), that is the supreme state. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4)
It should be restrained only so long as it has not reached dissolution within the heart;
this is both knowledge and liberation—anything other than this is merely an expansion of books.
Neither conceivable nor inconceivable, yet inconceivable and indeed conceivable—
when one is thus liberated from all partisan positions, one then attains Brahman.
One should unite with yoga by means of sound and contemplate the supreme beyond sound;
for through the state that is beyond sound, existence is not regarded as non-existence.
That very Brahman is partless, free from conceptual construction, and stainless;
having realized "I am that Brahman," one certainly attains Brahman. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 8)
Having known that which is free from conceptual construction, infinite, devoid of causes and examples, immeasurable, beginningless, and the supreme auspiciousness; BrbUp_9 //
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one to be honored nor a teaching,
neither the desire for liberation nor liberation— this is the ultimate reality.
The Self should be understood as one and the same throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
for one who has transcended these three stations, rebirth no longer exists.
For the single Self of all beings, residing in every being, is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.12)
Just as the space contained within a jar is not destroyed when the jar is dissolved,
but only the jar dissolves while the space remains, so too is the individual soul (jīva) comparable to the jar.
Like a jar, it is repeatedly broken into various forms;
yet that [Self] does not know itself as broken, and it knows eternally.
As long as one is enveloped by the illusion of sound, so long does one remain in the lotus;
but when darkness is pierced, one perceives the oneness that is truly one.
The syllable of sound is the supreme Brahman; when that has perished, that which remains is the Imperishable. If one desires peace for oneself, the wise man should meditate upon that Imperishable.
Two forms of knowledge are to be known: the Brahman of sound and that which is the Supreme.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the Supreme Brahman. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17)

Having studied the scripture, the wise man, through the true nature of theoretical and practical knowledge, should discard the scripture entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 18)
Just as the milk of cows of many different colors is of a single color,
one perceives knowledge to be like the milk, while the possessor of the marks (the individual soul) is like the cows.
Like clarified butter hidden in milk, consciousness dwells within every single being;
it must be constantly churned with the mind serving as the churning stick.
Having taken up the eye of knowledge, one should thereafter proceed toward the fire;
that which is partless, stainless, and tranquil is remembered as "I am Brahman. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 21)
And because I am the abode of all beings, dwelling within all beings through my nature as the benefactor of all, I am Vāsudeva.
